title: Service container, providers and dependency injection

preview.what: How Laravel builds your objects for you: what a binding is, when singletons are right, what providers do, and how a type-hint turns into a real object.
preview.picture: A hotel concierge. You say 'I need a payment gateway' and one arrives, already configured, without you knowing which company was called or how.
preview.why: 'How does Laravel know what to inject?' is the classic Laravel senior opener. The follow-ups — singleton vs bind, register vs boot, contextual binding — separate people who use Laravel from people who understand it.
preview.bn: Laravel কীভাবে তোমার object বানিয়ে দেয়: binding কী, singleton কখন, provider কী করে, type-hint থেকে object কীভাবে আসে।

lesson.problem: A controller does `new StripeGateway(config('stripe.key'))` in three places. The client switches to bKash; you change three files and miss a fourth in a queued job. Tests hit the real Stripe API because there's no way to swap it. Later, someone binds a per-request object as a singleton and a user sees another user's cart. All of this is the container's job, done by hand, badly.
lesson.picture: A hotel concierge desk. You don't go to the kitchen, the garage and the laundry yourself. You say 'I need a car' and the concierge knows which company to call, what to tell them, and hands you keys. The concierge is the container. The list of 'when someone asks for a car, call this company' is the bindings. Service providers are the staff who write that list before the hotel opens. Type-hinting `PaymentGateway $gateway` in a constructor is you telling the concierge what you need — you never say how.
lesson.hook: Ask for what you need by type. The container decides how. Providers write the rules before the first request.
lesson.concept:
**The container** is a registry of 'how to build X'. `app(Foo::class)` or `resolve(Foo::class)` asks it for X. If there's no binding, it **auto-wires**: reflects on Foo's constructor, resolves each type-hinted parameter recursively, and builds it. This is why most classes need no binding at all — concrete classes with typed constructors just work.

**When you must bind:** interfaces (the container can't instantiate an interface), classes that need config values, third-party clients, and anything you want to swap in tests.

```php
$this->app->bind(PaymentGateway::class, BkashGateway::class);       // new instance every resolve
$this->app->singleton(PaymentGateway::class, fn ($app) => new BkashGateway(config('services.bkash')));  // one instance per request lifecycle
$this->app->scoped(CurrentTenant::class, fn () => ...);              // one instance per request, reset between Octane requests
$this->app->instance(Clock::class, $fakeClock);                      // an existing object
```

**bind vs singleton vs scoped.** `bind`: a fresh object each time — safe default for anything holding request-specific state. `singleton`: built once, shared — for stateless services and expensive clients (HTTP clients, parsers). `scoped`: like singleton but reset per request under Octane/queue workers — use it for 'current user/tenant' style objects. The classic bug: singleton for something that holds user data; under Octane the second request sees the first user's data.

**Contextual binding** — the same interface, different implementation depending on who asks:
```php
$this->app->when(InvoiceService::class)->needs(Filesystem::class)->give(fn () => Storage::disk('invoices'));
$this->app->when(ReportService::class)->needs(Filesystem::class)->give(fn () => Storage::disk('reports'));
```
Also `->needs('$apiKey')->give(config(...))` for primitive constructor params, and `#[Config('services.bkash.key')]`-style attributes in Laravel 11+.

**Service providers.** Each has `register()` and `boot()`. Laravel calls `register()` on *every* provider first, then `boot()` on every provider. So: in `register()` only put bindings — other services may not exist yet. In `boot()` you may use anything: routes, policies, event listeners, macros, `Model::preventLazyLoading`, view composers. Deferred providers (`DeferrableProvider`) are loaded only when one of their bindings is requested — for heavy packages.

**Where injection happens:** constructors of controllers, jobs, listeners, middleware, commands; controller *method* parameters; closures passed to `app()->call()`. Facades are a static face over `app('name')`; `Cache::get()` is `app('cache')->get()`. Real-time facades (`Facades\App\Services\Foo`) are the same trick for your own classes.

**Method injection + route model binding** coexist: `public function show(Request $request, Order $order)` — Request comes from the container, Order from the route parameter.

**Testing** is the payoff: `$this->app->instance(PaymentGateway::class, new FakeGateway())` or `$this->mock(PaymentGateway::class)` and every consumer gets the fake without knowing.

**Anti-patterns:** `app()->make()` sprinkled inside business code (service locator — hides dependencies); `new` on collaborators inside classes; binding in `boot()` (works, but breaks the register/boot contract other packages rely on); giant `AppServiceProvider` — split providers by domain.
lesson.simple:
Imagine you're a chef and you shout 'I need a knife!' You don't say which drawer, which brand. A helper hands you a knife. The helper is the container. Before the restaurant opened, the manager wrote on a board: 'knife → the Japanese ones in drawer 3', 'oven → the big one'. That board is the bindings, and the manager writing it is a service provider's `register()`. When the restaurant is open and the manager turns on the lights and the music, that's `boot()` — you can only do that after everything is in place.

'Singleton' means there's exactly one big oven and everyone shares it. Fine for an oven. Terrible for a plate — if everyone shares one plate, your food ends up on someone else's table. Request-specific things are plates: make a new one each time.

When you want to test a recipe without turning on the real oven, you tell the helper 'today, oven means this toy oven'. Every recipe that asks for an oven gets the toy. That's why asking-by-type is powerful: you can swap the real thing for a fake in one line.

wrong.why: `new` in the controller means every consumer changes when the gateway changes and tests hit real APIs. `app(Cart::class)` inside the method hides that the controller needs a Cart. A singleton holding the user's cart leaks across requests under Octane/queues. Using the router in register() breaks when provider order changes.

right.why: One place decides which gateway exists; every consumer asks by interface. singleton for the stateless client, scoped for the per-user cart. boot() uses the Gate and Model classes safely because all providers have registered. Tests replace the binding with one line.

lesson.bn: Container = 'X কীভাবে বানাবো' তার registry। Binding না থাকলে auto-wire: constructor-এর type-hint দেখে নিজে বানায় — তাই বেশিরভাগ class-এ binding লাগে না। Binding লাগে interface-এ, config লাগলে, third-party client-এ, test-এ বদলাতে চাইলে। bind = প্রতিবার নতুন (request-এর data থাকলে এটাই); singleton = একবার বানিয়ে শেয়ার (stateless, দামি client); scoped = প্রতি request-এ এক, Octane-এ reset (current user/tenant)। Singleton-এ user-এর data রাখলে Octane-এ অন্য user-এর data দেখা যায়। Contextual binding: কে চাইছে তার ওপর ভিন্ন implementation। Provider: register() = শুধু binding, অন্য service নেই; boot() = সব provider register হয়ে গেছে, route/policy/listener দাও। Facade = app('name')-এর static মুখ। Test-এ $this->app->instance() বা $this->mock() দিয়ে এক লাইনে বদলাও। app()->make() business code-এ ছড়িও না।

versions.what: scoped() binding added (per-request singleton safe for Octane); native type hints across the framework; invokable validation rules.
versions.why_it_matters: scoped vs singleton is the Octane-safety question.

versions.what: Slim skeleton: config/app.php providers array gone, providers registered in bootstrap/providers.php; middleware configured in bootstrap/app.php; Kernel.php files removed; #[Config], #[Give], #[Tag], #[Auth] contextual attributes for constructor injection.
versions.why_it_matters: If you say 'add it to config/app.php providers' in a Laravel 11+ interview, you date yourself.

versions.what: No container semantics changes; maintenance release focused on dependency updates and new starter kits.
versions.why_it_matters: You can say the container has been stable since 10; the packaging around it changed in 11.

practice.task: In your prep-app: create interface App\Contracts\SmsSender with send(string $to, string $body): void, two implementations (LogSmsSender that writes to the log, FakeSmsSender that stores messages in an array), bind by config value, inject it into an artisan command sms:test that sends one message, and write a feature test that swaps in FakeSmsSender and asserts the message was 'sent'.
practice.hint: Provider register() with a match on config('services.sms.driver'); test uses $this->app->instance().
practice.why: Command handle() gets method injection from the container. The test replaces the binding with a real object, so no mocking library is needed and the assertion reads like plain PHP. This is the full loop: interface → binding → injection → swap in test.

practice.task: Bug hunt. A singleton CurrentTenant is resolved from the request's X-Tenant header. Under php artisan serve it works; under Octane, the second request sometimes sees the first request's tenant. Explain and fix with the smallest change.
practice.why: This exact bug is the standard 'have you actually run Octane' interview question, and it also bites long-running queue workers. Knowing the three lifetimes and which data belongs to which is the whole answer.

practice.task: Two report services need different filesystem disks but both type-hint Illuminate\Contracts\Filesystem\Filesystem. Write the contextual bindings, then explain why you did NOT create two interfaces.
practice.why: Contextual binding is the container feature most people have never used; being able to explain when it's better than a new interface is a senior-level distinction.

interview.q: How does Laravel know what to inject into a controller constructor?
interview.model: The container resolves the controller. It reflects on the constructor, and for each type-hinted parameter it checks its bindings — if there's a binding it uses it, otherwise it auto-wires by recursively constructing the concrete class. Interfaces must be bound because they can't be instantiated; concrete classes usually need nothing. Bindings are registered in service providers' register() methods, and the same mechanism handles method injection on controller actions, jobs, listeners and commands.
interview.missing: Mention reflection explicitly and that it's cached in production — shows you know there's a cost and that it's handled.
interview.followUp: What happens if a constructor parameter is a string like $apiKey?
interview.bn: Container controller বানায়: constructor reflect করে, প্রতিটা type-hint-এর binding দেখে, না থাকলে concrete class নিজে বানায় (auto-wire); interface-এ binding লাগবেই।

interview.q: bind vs singleton vs scoped — when do you use each?
interview.model: bind gives a new instance every resolve — my default for anything that holds per-operation state. singleton builds once and shares — for stateless services and expensive clients like an HTTP client. scoped is a singleton for the duration of one request and is flushed between requests under Octane and queue workers — for objects derived from the request or user, like current tenant or cart. The bug to avoid is a singleton holding user data: under Octane it leaks to the next request.
interview.missing: Give the FPM detail: under PHP-FPM singleton and scoped behave the same because the process dies per request — which is why the bug only shows up on Octane.
interview.followUp: Where else besides Octane does a long-lived container bite you?
interview.bn: bind = প্রতিবার নতুন; singleton = একবার, শেয়ার (stateless/দামি); scoped = প্রতি request-এ এক, Octane-এ flush (current user/tenant)।

interview.q: register() vs boot() in a service provider?
interview.model: Laravel runs register() on every provider first, then boot() on every provider. In register() I only bind things into the container, because other providers' services may not exist yet. In boot() everything is registered, so I can use the router, gates, events, models, and other services. Registering routes or listeners in register() works by luck and breaks when provider order changes.
interview.missing: Add deferred providers: they aren't loaded until one of their bindings is requested, which is how heavy packages avoid slowing every request.
interview.followUp: What's the difference between a provider's boot() and the booted() callback?
interview.bn: সব provider-এর register() আগে, তারপর সব boot(); register()-এ শুধু binding, boot()-এ router/gate/event/model ব্যবহার করা যায়।

interview.q: How do you test code that depends on a payment gateway without calling the real API?
interview.model: The code depends on a PaymentGateway interface, not a concrete class, so in the test I bind a fake — $this->app->instance(PaymentGateway::class, new FakeGateway()) or $this->mock() — and every consumer gets it through the container. The fake records calls so I can assert on them. That's the whole reason for injecting by interface; no dependency injection, no cheap fakes.
interview.missing: Distinguish fake (a real simple implementation) from mock (expectations on calls) and say when you prefer each.
interview.followUp: How would you make sure the real gateway is never called in CI?
interview.bn: Interface-এ depend করি, test-এ $this->app->instance() বা $this->mock() দিয়ে fake bind — সব consumer container থেকে fake পায়।

cards.q: What does the container do when there's no binding for a class?
cards.a: Auto-wires: reflects the constructor, resolves each type-hinted dependency recursively, builds the object.
Interfaces, classes needing config values, third-party clients, anything you want to swap in tests.

cards.q: bind / singleton / scoped in one line each
cards.a: bind: new each time. singleton: one shared instance. scoped: one per request, flushed under Octane/queue workers.
A singleton holding request/user data is reused by the next request — use scoped for anything derived from the request.
register(): bindings only, other services may not exist. boot(): all providers registered; routes, gates, listeners, macros go here.
when(Consumer)->needs(Contract)->give(impl): same interface, different implementation depending on who asks.
A static proxy to a container binding: Cache::get() is app('cache')->get().

cards.q: How do you swap a dependency in a test?
Laravel 11: where are providers and middleware registered?
cards.a: bootstrap/providers.php and bootstrap/app.php — config/app.php providers array and Kernel.php are gone.

glossary.bn: Laravel-এর registry যা object বানিয়ে দেয়।

glossary.plain: A rule: 'when someone asks for X, build it like this'.
The container building a class by reading its constructor's type-hints.
glossary.bn: Constructor-এর type-hint পড়ে container-এর নিজে বানানো।

glossary.plain: A class that registers bindings (register) and sets things up (boot) at startup.
glossary.bn: Startup-এ binding দেয় (register) আর সাজায় (boot) এমন class।
